To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

glyphosate applied at the field rate did not affect microbial biomass, fungal hyphales, bacterial:fungal ratios, bacterial and fungal phospho-lipid fatty acids, and bacterial and fungal community structures in the clay soil and sandy loam soil, whereas glyphosate applied at 100 times field rate resulted in a short-term stimulation of bacterial biomass, bacterial:fungal ratio, culturable bacteria and functional diversity in both soils, but did not affect the fungal community structure.

glyphosate applied to forest soils at the recommended field application rate did not affect the microbial community, but at a high concentration, the herbicide stimulated bacteria and shifted the microbial community structure from fungal dominance to a more balanced community.

(1) Glyphosate at a high concentration stimulated the bacterial community and increased bacterial:fungal biomass ratios, but did not change the fungal community; (2) Glyphosate at the field rate did not change the bacterial or fungal community; and (3) Changes in the bacterial community were transient, and the bacterial community was dominated by generalist bacteria.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of glyphosate on soil microorganisms, particularly bacteria.
the effect of herbicide on the microbial community structure.
understanding the role of soil microorganisms in the biogeochemical cycling of nutrients and contaminants in forest ecosystems.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the glyphosate-based herbicide Roundup does not affect soil microbial communities at field-relevant concentrations, but it does affect soil microbial communities in an uncontrolled and unpredictable manner at concentrations that are not relevant for the field.
glyphosate is not toxic to soil microorganisms.
glyphosate has a very limited effect on soil microbial communities.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the glyphosate herbicide is not a threat to the soil microbial communities in our forests.
glyphosate is not a selective herbicide for bacteria and fungi.
glyphosate, when applied at the field rate to forest soils, has a negligible impact on the microbial community.
The main takeaway from our work is that
glyphosate is not a microbial toxin at the field rate.
glyphosate is not toxic to soil microbial communities at the field rates that are applied to control weeds.
the recommended rate of glyphosate is not going to have any impact on the microbial community.
